integrator_questions: Is a 12 mm sensor spacing enough to resolve the line on tight bends, or do readings saturate or drop to zero across the array?
Does 60 mm lookahead give usable phase margin, or does it cause oscillation that the controller has to damp with kd?
Is the mass and track width giving enough turn authority without slip, and where do the largest errors occur?

intent: Baseline geometry: a five-sensor forward array with 12 mm spacing, 60 mm lookahead, 12 mm sensors, and a moderate 0.12 m track, 0.03 m wheels and 0.8 kg mass. Expected result: completion on the oval and s-bend, with a few line-loss events on the slalom. The purpose is to measure how the array behaves so that later iterations can tune spacing, lookahead and track width against real data.
learning: No evidence yet. Hypotheses to test: (1) lookahead of 60 mm improves curve tracking over 30 mm at the cost of some jitter; (2) 12 mm spacing is a good balance between resolution and coverage; (3) the wheel track of 0.12 m is adequate for the required speed without excessive slip.
rationale: Iteration 0 has no race telemetry or Integrator feedback, so this is a neutral baseline built from the contract. Five sensors at 12 mm spacing span 48 mm across the front of the body. That is wider than the 25 mm tape, so the line stays visible across the array during bends and small lateral errors, and the centre-of-array reading gives a usable signal for weighted-average steering. The sensors sit 60 mm ahead of the axle to give lookahead, which helps on curves, but not at the 80 mm limit, which would add lag and sensitivity to noise. Sensor size is 12 mm, a middle choice that covers part of the tape in every sensor so readings change smoothly as the robot moves. Wheel track is 0.12 m and wheel radius 0.03 m, a moderate turn authority with a common ground speed. Body width of 0.12 m keeps the off-track limit at its 0.06 m floor, which is comparable to the tape-plus-quarter-body value. Mass of 0.8 kg and a 0.18 m body length give moderate yaw inertia, so the robot can turn without sluggishness. I expect this to complete the development tracks with a few line-loss events at most, but the real test is the first race. The most likely failure modes are overshoot on the slalom and loss of the line on sharp bends, and the race data should show which.
